newsitem.title: UK: Fundamentalist Islamic London rally sparks protest.
newsitem.headline: Fundamentalist Islamic London rally sparks protest.

text.p: Britain faced sharp criticism from foreign governments ahead of Sunday's "Rally for Revival" organised by an Islamic fundamentalist group and featuring messages from some of the world's most militant Islamic leaders.

The government issued a stern warning to al-Muhajiroun, a group that had called for a holy war against governments in the Middle East, that it would not tolerate statements supporting terrorism -- but said it had no legal grounds to stop the rally.

"There aren't any powers for the home secretary (interior minister) or the police to ban the rally. We will be monitoring the meeting and anyone who breaks the law will be prosecuted," a government spokesman said.
"The British government condemns any statement made at the rally in support of terrorism, or violence more generally. We will ensure that the rule of law in this country is upheld."
Moslem academics and representatives from many Islamic movements around the world plan to attend the one-day rally.
Omar Abdul-Rahman, the 65-year-old sheikh who was jailed for life for his part in the bombing of the World Trade Centre in New York, will address the conference in a pre-recorded video.

Osama Bin Laden, who has called for a holy war against Americans in Saudi Arabia, and Mohammad Hussein Fadhlullah, spiritual lader of the Hizbollah group in Lebanon, have been banned from entering Britain to attend the conference. Both men are scheduled to talk to delegates via a video link.
They are being restricted "on the grounds that their presence would not be conducive to the public good on the grounds of national security", the government spokesman said.
Egypt and Algeria, both fighting against internal Islamic threats, have urged Britain to stop the gathering at the 12,000-seat London Arena in the Docklands financial district.
"I am surprised at the holding of such a conference which will include many of those elements who encourage terrrorism," Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak said in Cairo.
Algeria described the rally as "a meeting bringing together masterminds and ideologists and financers of terrorism." Jewish groups in Britain have also voiced their concern.
Mohammad al-Masari, a London-based Saudi dissident who recently won his fight against deportation and has been criticised for calling for the annihilation of Jews, is also expected to be there.
The founder of al Muhajiroun, militant Syrian Omar Bakri Mohammed who has called for a worldwide Islamic state, gave assurances the rally will pose no danger.
"The message will not contain any anti-Semitic messages or any incitement to terrorism because that is against our principles," he said in a recent interview.

If nothing else, Sunday's rally will give credence to London's growing reputation in many overseas capitals as an overly tolerant city towards dissident groups, especially those with their roots in the Middle East.
It is home to tens of thousands of Moslem expatriates, many opposition groups have their headquarters in London and several Arab and Islamic newspapers are published here.
